If Voat is still based on Microsoft ASP.Net Core architecture (or really any MS internet server/app technology), a programmer can setup different app pools for different parts of a site so that they run independently and don't mess with each other's resources. This has been a common feature of MS Internet Information Server (Microsoft's web server) for the last 20 years. It's not magical and it's not exotic. Anyone with a little knowledge could setup app pools on a Microsoft server and those app pools will happily run even if other ones fail. All of you app pools can run on one domain on the same TCP port even. Like I said, it's old technology now and far from being unlikely to be used on a site like Voat.
Its not limited to MS tech. It's basic load balancing and occurs for any high traffic web server architecture.

MS App Pools aren't like like balancing at all. Load balancing involves multiple servers in a pool that share the request load of a site or application. App Pooling is more like process isolation and it happens on a single server. It executes the web application code in a separate memory space under separate threads and with isolation from other processes. It doesn't balance any loads and it happens on one server. It just a form of protecting processes from other processes so that they can coexist with each other even if one of them fails. I'm sure other web servers can do similar things, but MS has had this feature for a very long time now.
